# Interpolation Functions for Resampling

Also called: Cubic-spline

## Overview
This family defines the mathematical functions used to estimate continuous values between discrete samples for edge reconstruction and shading [S1, unofficial]. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific focus on the trade-off between grey-value reconstruction fidelity and edge location accuracy, particularly in medical imaging contexts where negative values or gradient errors produce visible artifacts [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family estimate a continuous function $V(\mathbf{p})$ from discrete samples $V_i$ at grid positions $\mathbf{p}_i$ [S1, unofficial]. The interpolation error depends on the sample distance relative to the point-spread function (PSF) width, growing approximately with the third power of the sample distance [S1, unofficial]. The choice of interpolation function determines the trade-off between grey-value reconstruction fidelity, edge location accuracy, and noise sensitivity [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Linear Interpolation
Linear interpolation performs better than cubic-spline but worse than quadratic re-sampling for edge location estimation [S1, unofficial].

### Quadratic Re-sampling
Quadratic re-sampling is less sensitive to noise compared to linear and cubic-spline functions [S1, unofficial]. For edge location estimation, it yields the smallest error, outperforming both linear and cubic methods [S1, unofficial].

### Cubic-spline Interpolation
Cubic-spline interpolation is often considered best for general grey-value reconstruction fidelity [S1, unofficial]. However, it causes overshoot in step responses, producing negative values which are invalid for MR data due to the complex modulus operator [S1, unofficial]. Consequently, it yields the largest edge location error among the compared functions [S1, unofficial].

### Edge location estimation via mean thresholding
This is a specific evaluation method and application of interpolation functions for determining the position of a 1D step edge [S1, unofficial]. It estimates the edge position by finding the coordinate where the re-sampled grey-value equals the arithmetic mean of the grey-values on both sides of the step [S1, unofficial]. The procedure involves: 1. Re-sampling discrete samples across the step using an interpolation function. 2. Computing the mean of the grey-values on the low and high sides of the step. 3. Locating the coordinate where the re-sampled curve intersects this mean value [S1, unofficial]. Quadratic re-sampling yields the smallest edge location error, linear interpolation performs better than cubic-spline but worse than quadratic, and cubic-spline interpolation yields the largest error [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The analysis focuses on edge reconstruction accuracy for CT and MR data, evaluating how different interpolation functions handle step edges and gradient estimation [S1, unofficial]. The work highlights that while cubic-spline is often preferred for visual smoothness, it introduces artifacts (ripples) and inaccuracies in edge detection due to overshoot and sample-distance-dependent errors [S1, unofficial]. The error in edge location estimation grows approximately with the third power of the sample distance, necessitating careful consideration of sampling rates relative to the point-spread function width [S1, unofficial].
